transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Start: 15:42 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Alex Rivera (Meridian Platform), Maya Chen (Meridian Security), Samir Patel (Meridian ML), Olivia Park (Meridian DevOps)

Summary:
Quickstart walkthrough focused on using GCP Workload Identity for auth with Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), environment setup for a sandbox project, brief demo of Redwood Console and Optimize suggestions, discussion on private networking and least-privileged service accounts. Agreed to a pilot benchmark next week.

Topics:
- GCP Workload Identity flow and service account impersonation
- SDK authentication patterns (env var vs workload identity vs keyfile)
- Sandbox provisioning and networking (VPC peering, egress, allowlist)
- Console walkthrough: model selection, routes, token breakdowns
- Optimize: batching, KV cache, quantization recommendations
- Security questions: KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML, SOC2

Timestamps and transcript (note: autogenerated transcript, some words may be off):
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. Quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE, and Priya is our SE who will do the deeper env and demo stuff.
[00:18] Alex: Hey all, Alex here. We're primarily trying to avoid key files in CI, so Workload Identity was top ask.
[00:25] Priya: Perfect, that's exactly what we planned. We'll show both python and TS flows. Also we'll touch on how Redwood Console surfaces cost/latency per-route so you can validate pilot success.
[00:45] Maya: Quick governance note — Meridan (sic) requires KMS-wrapped tokens in logs and a minimal blast radius for service accounts.
[00:53] Priya: Got it. We'll highlight IAM roles needed and KMS integration.
[01:12] Jordan: Agenda — 1) Walkthrough of Workload Identity mapping and sample manifests, 2) show SDK usage in Py and TS, 3) Console/Optimize quick tour, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[01:40] Priya: Okay jumping into the flow: on GCP you create a workload identity pool, then a provider that ties your cluster OIDC to a GCP service account. The application uses the Kubernetes service account annotated with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account to impersonate. This avoids storing JSON keys.
[02:05] Samir: How does Redwood authenticate to the model runtime? I mean do we still need a Redwood API key?
[02:13] Jordan: Short answer — yes, you need a Redwood API token for your account, but the recommendation for infra is to keep that token in a secret store and let the application read it from env during runtime; for CI/CD and cluster scenarios we prefer using Workload Identity to fetch short-lived creds coupled with KMS if you want additional encryption.
[02:36] Olivia: So is the token exchange automated if we run the Redwood agent on a private VPC?
[02:45] Priya: There's no separate agent required — for Redwood Private you run our runtime in your VPC or on-prem and you can wire auth into your existing KMS and IAM flows. For hosted we accept tokens over TLS; you can use short-lived tokens minted by your infra then rotated into the container at start.
[03:12] Alex: Can you show the python snippet? We tried something but got an "invalid token" error.
[03:18] Priya: Sure, I'll paste the quickstart link first: https://git.redwood.io/quickstarts/gcp-wi — contains sample manifests and py/ts examples.
[03:28] Priya: Python flow: set REDWOOD_API_TOKEN in env (or mount into container secret) and then from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_TOKEN')). For workload identity, our sample uses metadata server to swap for the token stored in Secret Manager; note there's a couple of permutations here.
[03:55] Maya: Wait, metadata server swap — isn't that GCE-specific? We run GKE with Workload Identity, we don't want node scopes.
[04:05] Priya: Right, metadata server patterns differ. For GKE with Workload Identity you annotate KSA and then the app calls the token exchange endpoint to get an access token scoped to the service account. Our sample shows a tiny init script that requests short-lived token and writes REDWOOD_API_TOKEN env var before starting the app.
[04:32] Samir: That's a little manual — any recommended sidecar pattern?
[04:37] Priya: Yes, we show both: an initContainer snippet and a small sidecar to refresh every 45 minutes. The sidecar approach is safer for long-running pods to avoid stale tokens.
[04:59] Jordan: One note on RBAC — you only need iam.serviceAccounts.actAs on the target GCP SA for the KSA to impersonate. Keep other roles scoped to read-only.
[05:20] Alex: Ok that explains our earlier error. We had the wrong impersonation role. Good catch.
[05:31] Priya: Moving to TypeScript — using the node SDK it's essentially identical: process.env.REDWOOD_API_TOKEN or if you prefer a credential provider, we show a small provider that uses the google-auth-library to fetch token and then passes to Redwood SDK.
[05:54] Olivia: For our CI — GitHub Actions — do you have a recommended pattern for ephemeral tokens?
[06:01] Priya: For GH Actions you can use Workload Identity Federation with a workload identity pool and short-lived service account tokens. Then the workflow fetches a token and writes it into the step env without persist. We have a sample GH Action in the repo.
[06:28] Maya: Security question — do Redwood logs ever contain full prompt text? We need to ensure PHI isn't sent to hosted unless redaction or allowlist is done.
[06:38] Jordan: Good question. Hosted API by default processes prompt text; we offer field-level redaction and configurable retention. For regulated data you can use Redwood Private or dedicated with audit logs stored in your KMS-backed bucket. We'll share the security datasheet.
[06:58] Samir: Ok on Optimize — will Optimize suggestions recommend quantization and batching settings per-model automatically?
[07:06] Priya: Yes, Optimize analyzes request patterns and suggests batching/batch limits, prefix KV caching, and quantization tiers if quality tradeoffs are acceptable. You can accept suggestions per-route in the Console.
[07:27] Alex: Can you demo the Console quickly?
[07:33] Priya: Yep — switching to screen: Console shows model catalog on left, routes in the center, token-level cost breakdown per route on hover. (transcription: brief pause) I will run a sample request.
[07:55] [screen noise] Priya: Here's a route configured to use a 4-bit quantized variant, batching window 50ms, prefix caching enabled. You can toggle model variant for canary and see latency histograms. Also Optimize tab shows recommendations and estimated $/1M tokens.
[08:30] Samir: That UI is nice. For the pilot we want to test latency at P50 and P95 for our 512-token median prompts — can Redwood run a synthetic benchmark against our model variant?
[08:42] Jordan: We can. We typically run a microbenchmark with your prompt corpus then compare hosted vs dedicated vs private numbers. We'll need an SSH or S3 drop for the corpus and service account access in sandbox.
[09:02] Alex: We'll prepare a redacted prompt set.
[09:08] Priya: Great. Also keep in mind continuous batching behavior — for low QPS workloads batching may add latency at the P95 tail; Optimize suggests appropriate batch windows to balance cost and tail latency.
[09:30] Maya: On network, if we use hosted but want egress to come from our VPC for allowlist, possible?
[09:36] Priya: We have VPC peering patterns and private egress via NAT. For strict allowlisting we often recommend Dedicated or Private because you can control egress IP ranges. Hosted can work with allowlist entries but with shared egress ranges — we can discuss the specific model later.
[09:57] Olivia: Any change to our infra for KV cache? We want to persist prefix caches to reduce token consumption across warm restarts.
[10:05] Priya: We support Redis-backed KV cache. For Private you can run it locally; for hosted we provide an ephemeral in-memory cache but persistent Redis is available as an add-on. In the quickstart we show how to mount redis connection string via Secret Manager and configure RedwoodClient(cache_url=...) in Python.
[10:30] Samir: We heard about "KV cash" earlier in a doc — haha — that's a typo I guess.
[10:35] Jordan: Yeah, KV "cash" — the docs have that one in a beta note, classic. We'll correct.
[10:44] [laughter]
[11:07] Priya: Now quick demo of an integration failure mode — I simulate expired token. (clicks) You can see 401 coming back with a header x-redwood-trace-id, which helps us correlate with logs in the Console. We recommend enabling request tracing during pilot.
[11:35] Samir: Does trace data contain prompt text?
[11:40] Jordan: By default tracing includes metadata and partial request hashes; payloads are redacted unless you opt-in. We log prompt hash for dedup and quality monitoring.
[12:02] Maya: For compliance — SOC2 and ISO — do you have certs?
[12:07] Jordan: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO 27001 — we'll send the attestation pack.
[12:16] Maya: Great, please share the report and the SOC controls mapping.
[12:20] Jordan: Noted.
[12:34] Olivia: Back to auth — any gotchas with node-based serverless functions calling Redwood?
[12:40] Priya: Serverless — you still want short-lived tokens. For Cloud Run we recommend Workload Identity Federation or attach a service account with limited scope then do direct exchange. Avoid embedding long-lived tokens in source.
[12:58] Alex: We also want to run an edge case where multiple microservices share a token store — is there a pattern to enforce per-route least privilege in Redwood?
[13:08] Priya: In Console you can attach route-level credentials and RBAC. If you want separation, create separate API tokens for each microservice and bind them to routes with token-level quotas.
[13:25] Samir: Ok, that's helpful.
[13:32] Jordan: Quick pause — any more auth questions before I continue?
[13:36] Maya: One more — does Redwood support HSM-backed KMS for token wrapping?
[13:42] Jordan: Yes, for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For hosted you can integrate via our partner KMS flows or use Redwood-managed KMS with contract terms — we'll detail in the security pack.
[13:58] Priya: Jumping back into sample manifests — showing a GKE manifest now: a Kubernetes service account annotated with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: meridian-svc@meridian-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com, plus RoleBinding for secrets access. We demonstrate minimal roles: iam.serviceAccounts.get and iam.serviceAccounts.actAs.
[14:30] Alex: We had an issue where the token exchange kept returning 403; we later found a missing cloud resource manager permission.
[14:38] Priya: Yep, the IAM graph can be surprising. We'll include a checklist in the repo that lists the exact required roles and common misconfigurations.
[14:50] Jordan: Quick note about PKCE for browser clients — if you call Redwood directly from the browser, use short-lived tokens and PKCE with your OIDC. But for our SDKs the typical server-to-server pattern is recommended.
[15:10] Olivia: For our front-end, we want to call a Redwood route that runs reranking — is there a recommended proxy pattern?
[15:17] Priya: Use a backend-for-frontend (BFF) that holds a route-level token and exposes limited endpoints to the browser. That keeps tokens off the client.
[15:30] Samir: What about request-level encryption at rest?
[15:35] Jordan: Audit logs and stored artifacts can be encrypted with your KMS in Private. Hosted data at rest is encrypted but you can request KMS integration for enterprise plans.
[15:50] Maya: Let's talk billing and token accounting quickly — we need clarity on how the Console breaks down costs.
[15:58] Jordan: Console shows token-level billing per-route and per-model. We also export CSV for finance systems. Optimize will estimate $/1M tokens for chosen config.
[16:18] Alex: Any pitfalls when moving from sandbox to dedicated?
[16:23] Priya: The main change is capacity guarantees and network isolation. You'll switch to dedicated endpoints and can pin model versions. Usually you adjust batch windows because throughput changes with dedicated GPU pools.
[16:42] Olivia: For the pilot, what's the minimal infra footprint?
[16:47] Priya: Sandbox: GKE cluster, a service account with actAs, one Redis instance for KV cache (optional), and a small S3/GCS bucket for logs. We provide terraform snippets in the repo.
[17:05] Jordan: We'll send an infra checklist after the call.
[17:12] Alex: Great.
[17:18] Priya: Now running a short demo: start a python container -- watch logs as it exchanges identity and makes a request to Redwood API. (typing) The sample repo uses an initContainer to write token to /etc/redwood/token, then main reads it.
[17:45] Samir: Can you show the sidecar refresh?
[17:50] Priya: Sure, sidecar hits STS endpoint every 40 minutes, writes new token. We also show a health endpoint so liveness probes know when token swap fails.
[18:09] Alex: That's useful. We'll probably adopt the sidecar.
[18:16] Maya: On the subject of redaction — can Redwood perform PII scrubbing before storing prompts in logs?
[18:23] Jordan: We have configurable scrubbers and pre-send filters for hosted. For Private you can plug in your own preprocessor. We'll include a sample preprocessor in the repo.
[18:40] Priya: Quick note about latency when using Redis KV cache across AZs — you'll get added network latency. Prefer colocated caches in the same AZ as runtime for best results.
[18:55] Olivia: For our HA strategy, do you recommend multiple service accounts per cluster or a single impersonation identity?
[19:02] Priya: Multiple service accounts map to better isolation; single SA is simpler but increases blast radius. We recommend per-namespace SA for critical services.
[19:18] Jordan: Jumping forward — pilot timeline: provision sandbox (Meridian) -> run benchmark -> review Optimize suggestions -> iterate.
[19:27] Alex: Sounds good.
[19:33] Priya: Any pressing legal/procurement items?
[19:36] Maya: We'll need SLAs and data residency language for our procurement team; otherwise this is fine.
[19:44] Jordan: We'll attach standard SLA addendum and data residency notes to the deal folder.
[19:52] Samir: About monitoring — how do we get logs into our Datadog?
[19:58] Priya: We can stream logs via our logging integration; we also export traces. We'll send the integration guide.
[20:12] Olivia: One last infra question — if we run Redwood Private on-prem, does the runtime require GPUs?
[20:18] Priya: If you run large models you need GPUs; for small reranking or embeddings you can run on CPU. The runtime supports quantized models to reduce GPU needs.
[20:35] Jordan: Okay let's move to recap and concrete next steps.
[20:40] Recap: 1) Jordan to share quickstart repo + security pack; 2) Priya to provide k8s manifests + sidecar examples; 3) Customer to provision sandbox and share prompts; 4) Schedule pilot benchmark for 2025-03-25.
[21:05] Alex: Quick question — can we get a preconfigured sandbox with limited traffic allowed from our corporate IP?
[21:12] Jordan: Yes, we can spin a sandbox with allowlist; we'll include that as part of the pilot provisioning.
[21:22] Maya: Please make sure the sandbox has KMS integration enabled.
[21:26] Jordan: Noted.
[21:30] Priya: Any final questions?
[21:33] Samir: Not for now.
[21:36] Olivia: none here.
[21:40] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the repo link and checklist.
[21:46] [meeting ends — transcription cuts off; remaining minutes used for post-call chat and quick infra notes]
